title: When is Wideframe not the right tool for your video workflow?
summary: Understand when Wideframe fits an Apple Silicon and Premiere workflow, and when transcript editing, simple clipping, or another existing tool is enough.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Check platform and finishing requirements before comparing creative features.
- Use your existing editor when it already solves the immediate task.
- Add an assistant for a recurring source-preparation need, not an imagined future use.


## Your current platform may decide the answer


Wideframe's[published requirements](https://try.wideframe.com/pricing/) specify an Apple Silicon Mac, M1 or newer, and Premiere Pro. If those are not part of your working setup, do not assume a Windows workflow, an Intel Mac, or a different finishing editor is an equivalent supported path.


A mixed-platform team may still have an appropriate Mac-based editor, but that is a team workflow decision. Confirm who operates the product and how the sources and deliverables move. Do not buy it on the assumption that team pricing means every platform or collaborative handoff is automatically supported.


## You may only need a simple edit


If the job is trimming a known passage and adding a title, the editor you already use may be enough. A source-preparation assistant becomes more relevant when you need help finding material, organizing it, or repeatedly preparing editable work from a brief.


An illustrative one-off task is cutting a short approved answer from a finished customer interview. You may not need to ingest a broader library or create a new workflow. Start with the simplest tool that can produce the actual delivery, especially when the task will not recur.


## A transcript-focused workflow may suit the person editing


If your team wants to shape a known recording primarily by editing words, consider a transcript-centered workflow.[Descript documents text-based editing](https://www.descript.com/video-editing) , and[Premiere has its own text-based editing features](https://helpx.adobe.com/sg/premiere/desktop/edit-projects/edit-video-using-text-based-editing/overview-of-text-based-editing.html) . Neither should be dismissed simply because an assistant is available elsewhere.


Wideframe becomes a stronger consideration when the work begins with a broader source question and the team wants prepared material in Premiere. Choose according to what the person will do repeatedly, not an assumed hierarchy in which every more complex workflow is better.


## A finished video may need clipping, not a new assembly


An already approved long video contains editorial decisions you may want to preserve. If you need excerpts for distribution, a clipping or repurposing workflow can be the right next stage. You do not need to reconstruct the source story merely to shorten it.


By contrast, a folder of customer interviews and supporting footage may not yet contain a coherent story. That is where source search and assembly preparation have a clearer role. The same team can use different tools at those different stages without making either purchase a universal replacement.


## Unresolved source or handling requirements come first


If you do not have the footage, the rights to use it, or clarity about the permitted processing workflow, resolve that before giving a tool access. A desktop application is not itself a complete answer about processing destinations and data handling.


This is especially relevant for teams with contractual requirements. Get the specific information needed for your use rather than assuming that a local folder means every operation remains on the device. The right buying decision can be to wait until a material requirement is answered.


## When the fit is clear, start with source work


If you have the appropriate setup and a recurring source-preparation task, begin with the relevant footage folder and a real brief. Wideframe's[soundbite workflow](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/find-soundbites/) is one concrete starting point for interview work. Use the public recipe in a new chat to add the task when needed.


Ask for a useful selection and take it into your normal Premiere finish. The purpose is to complete work already on your schedule, such as finding customer answers for a current story. That is a better reason to subscribe than a vague plan to automate all editing later.


## Keep the choice open as your work changes


A tool that is unnecessary for today's simple cut may become useful when a team starts producing recurring interviews. Conversely, a source-preparation subscription may matter less during a month of work that contains little source discovery. Revisit the decision without treating it as a permanent identity.


The right outcome is a workflow the team understands and uses. Keep Wideframe when it has a clear recurring job beside Premiere. Choose another approach when the input, platform, operator, or required output points elsewhere.
